nodes.label: Britain
nodes.full: The one enemy France never beats: it bankrolls every coalition, fights the Haitian war, is the target of the Continental System, sends Wellington to bleed the Grande Armée in Spain, and stands with Blücher at Waterloo.
nodes.src: background — Esdaile, 'The Peninsular War' (2003); Crouzet (1964)

nodes.label: The Continental Powers
nodes.full: Austria, Prussia and Russia: turned back at Valmy, broken at Austerlitz, their Holy Roman Empire dissolved and their map redrawn, they regather army after army until Prussia's Blücher reaches the field at Waterloo.
nodes.src: background — Chandler, 'The Campaigns of Napoleon' (1966); Broers, 'Europe Under Napoleon' (2002)

nodes.label: The Papacy
nodes.full: Rome: Pius VI condemns the Civil Constitution of the Clergy in 1791, Pius VII signs the Concordat that heals the schism in 1801 and attends the coronation, and is later imprisoned by the Emperor he crowned.
nodes.src: background — McManners, 'The French Revolution and the Church' (1972); Ellis, 'Napoleon' (2000)

nodes.label: Louis XVI — from king to prisoner
nodes.full: Louis XVI moves from Versailles to Paris under popular pressure in October 1789 — his flight to Varennes in June 1791 destroys his credibility; the storming of the Tuileries (10 August 1792) ends the monarchy; he is executed on 21 January 1793.
nodes.src: Louis XVI's diary entry for 14 Jul 1789: 'Rien' — Archives nationales KK 622. The flight to Varennes 20–21 Jun 1791: documented in eyewitness accounts and official records. The trial records: Archives nationales, série W 293. The execution 21 Jan 1793: Moniteur Universel 22 Jan 1793 (BnF). Jordan (1979), The King's Trial: the standard study of Louis XVI's trial.

nodes.label: The Republic — from the Convention to the Directory
nodes.full: The First Republic passes through the Terror (1793–1794), Thermidor, and the Directory — five years of political violence, dechristianisation, revolutionary war and corruption; the Revolutionary archive is one of the richest primary source collections in European history.
nodes.src: Archives parlementaires (1789–1860): the verbatim record of the Revolutionary assemblies — digitised by Stanford/BnF (French Revolution Digital Archive). The Moniteur Universel (official newspaper of the Revolution): BnF Gallica. The Terror's records: Archives nationales, Tribunal Révolutionnaire série W. Schama (1989), Citizens: A Chronicle of the French Revolution: the standard narrative history.

nodes.label: Napoleon Bonaparte — from First Consul to Emperor
nodes.full: Napoleon seizes power in the coup of 18 Brumaire — rules as First Consul (1799–1804) then Emperor; his Civil Code (1804), prefectural system and Concordat with the Church reshape France permanently; defeated at Waterloo on 18 June 1815 he abdicates a second time.
nodes.src: Napoleon's correspondence: published in 32 volumes (1858–1870) by the Commission Impériale; over 20,000 letters. Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène (1823): Napoleon's own retrospective account — BnF. The Civil Code (Code Napoléon): Bulletin des Lois 1804. Waterloo: 18 Jun 1815 confirmed in military records on both sides. Tulard (1977), Napoléon ou le mythe du sauveur: the standard French biography.

nodes.label: Haitian Revolution — enslaved people overthrow slavery
nodes.full: The enslaved population of Saint-Domingue rises on 22 August 1791 — the only successful slave revolution in history; after 13 years of war against France, Spain and Britain, Haiti declares independence on 1 January 1804; Napoleon sends an expedition that fails disastrously.
nodes.src: The night of 22 Aug 1791: documented in colonial records (ANOM) and contemporary white colonist accounts. The Declaration of Independence 1 Jan 1804: original document (Haitian National Archives). Napoleon's expedition: Archives de la Guerre A1 and Archives nationales, Colonies CC9. Dubois (2004), Avengers of the New World: the standard modern history using French, Haitian and British archives.

nodes.label: Valmy — the Revolution defends itself
nodes.full: The revolutionary army stops the Prussian-Austrian invasion at Valmy — a cannonade that barely touches either side; but the Prussians retreat; Goethe (present as an observer) remarks 'From this place and from this day forth commences a new era in the world's history'.
nodes.src: Kellermann's dispatches: Archives de la Guerre A1. Goethe's account: Campagne in Frankreich (1822) — he was an eyewitness. The battle's minor tactical significance vs enormous symbolic importance: documented in all contemporary accounts. Moniteur Universel 24 Sep 1792: BnF. Forrest (2011), Napoleon's Men: analyses the Revolutionary army's social composition.

nodes.label: The Terror — 16,594 official executions
nodes.full: The Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre executes 16,594 people by guillotine (official figure) and perhaps 40,000 in total including mass drownings (noyades) in Nantes and shootings in Lyon; the Tribunal Révolutionnaire records survive as a primary source of extraordinary completeness.
nodes.src: Tribunal Révolutionnaire records: Archives nationales, série W — the most complete record of any mass political execution in European history. The 16,594 official figure: Greer (1935), The Incidence of the Terror. Noyades in Nantes: documented in Carrier's dispatches (Archives nationales) and local records. Linton (2013), Choosing Terror: uses the tribunal records. Robespierre's fall 9 Thermidor (27 Jul 1794): Convention records (Archives parlementaires).

nodes.label: War in the Vendée — the Revolution's bloodiest internal conflict
nodes.full: Counter-revolutionary peasant uprising against conscription and dechristianisation — the Republican army uses the 'infernal columns' of General Turreau, burning villages and killing civilians; an estimated 170,000–200,000 die; the most devastating internal military conflict of the Revolution; still contested in France (the Vendée debates genocide classification).
nodes.src: General Turreau's 'infernal columns' dispatches (February 1794): Archives de la Guerre A1. Parish burial records (mass graves): documented in departmental archives of Vendée and Maine-et-Loire. Martin (1987), La Vendée de la mémoire: the standard modern study. Secher (1986), Le Génocide franco-français: the contested 'genocide' argument. The casualty estimate 170,000–200,000: Reynald Secher's figure — debated by Martin (1987) who argues lower. The primary legislative trigger: the levée en masse decree of 23 February 1793 — documented.

nodes.label: Austerlitz — Napoleon's greatest victory
nodes.full: Napoleon defeats the combined Austrian-Russian army in less than a day at Austerlitz — his most brilliant tactical victory; he dictates the subsequent peace terms from the battlefield; the Emperor's 18th Bulletin (3 Dec 1805) is his own account.
nodes.src: Napoleon's Bulletins de la Grande Armée (official campaign bulletins): Archives nationales, AF IV. Austrian military records: Kriegsarchiv, Vienna. Russian military records: RGVIA, Moscow. Austrian-Russian casualties: c.36,000 vs French c.9,000 — documented in after-action reports. Chandler (1966), The Campaigns of Napoleon: the standard modern tactical study.

nodes.label: Peninsular War — Napoleon's 'Spanish ulcer'
nodes.full: Napoleon's attempt to replace the Spanish Bourbons triggers a popular guerrilla war — the Peninsular War ties down 300,000 French troops for six years; the guerrilla (the word enters European languages from this war) and Wellington's forces bleed the Grande Armée; Napoleon calls it 'my Spanish ulcer'; the military catalyst for his decline.
nodes.src: Napoleon's 'ulcère espagnol': Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène Vol.II — documented. French military records: Archives de la Guerre A1 (Spain series). Wellington's dispatches: British National Archives WO 1. Esdaile (2003), The Peninsular War: the standard modern study. The troop commitment: 300,000 French soldiers documented in Archives de la Guerre. The word 'guerrilla': first enters English military usage from Spanish reports — documented in the OED (1809 first usage).

nodes.label: Waterloo — the final defeat
nodes.full: Napoleon's final battle — Wellington and Blücher defeat him in 8 hours; 47,000 casualties in one day; Napoleon abdicates four days later; the battle is the most documented military engagement of the 19th century, with eyewitness accounts from hundreds of participants.
nodes.src: Wellington's dispatches: British National Archives, WO 1/337 (his Waterloo despatch). Napoleon's abdication 22 Jun 1815: Archives nationales. Victor Hugo's Les Misérables (1862), the Waterloo chapter: a literary reconstruction but based on direct testimony from veterans. Roberts (2005), Waterloo: Napoleon's Last Gamble: uses archives on both sides. The battlefield: extant (UNESCO Memory of the World for the associated records).

nodes.label: Declaration of the Rights of Man — 26 August 1789
nodes.full: The National Assembly adopts the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen on 26 August 1789 — 17 articles establishing natural rights, national sovereignty and the rule of law; it is the foundational document of modern human rights and directly influenced the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948).
nodes.src: HARD ANCHOR: Original text: Archives nationales (AE/I/12). The vote on 26 Aug 1789: Archives parlementaires Vol.VIII (digitised). The Declaration's influence on the UDHR (1948): documented in the UN drafting committee records. Hunt (1996), The French Revolution and Human Rights: documentary anthology. The French Revolution Digital Archive (Stanford/BnF): digitised primary sources.

nodes.label: August Decrees (4–11 Aug 1789) — abolition of the feudal regime
nodes.full: On the night of 4 August 1789, in a cascade of renunciations, the National Assembly abolishes tithes, seignorial rights, venality of offices, and aristocratic privileges — the feudal regime is destroyed in a single night; the August Decrees are the legal foundation of modern France, as structurally important as the Declaration of Rights but less celebrated.
nodes.src: August Decrees: Archives parlementaires, Vol.VIII — the verbatim record. Published: Gaceta de la Régence. Markoff (1996), The Abolition of Feudalism: the standard modern study, using both the décrets and the cahiers de doléances. The night of 4 August: documented in the Archives parlementaires — the cascade of voluntary renunciations by nobles. The connection to the cahiers de doléances (lists of grievances): Markoff documents the peasant demands that the decrees answered.

nodes.label: Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 Jul 1790) — the fractured nation
nodes.full: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy turns priests into salaried public servants elected by their parishioners and requires an oath of loyalty to the constitution — the resulting split between juror priests (who swear) and refractory priests (who refuse) alienates millions of devout Catholics, drives the peasantry into counter-revolution, and is the primary cause of the Vendée uprising.
nodes.src: Civil Constitution of the Clergy 12 Jul 1790: Archives parlementaires; Moniteur Universel 13 Jul 1790 (BnF). The oath requirement (27 Nov 1790): documented. The split statistics: approximately 55% of priests swear, 45% refuse — documented in departmental records. McManners (1972), The French Revolution and the Church: the standard study. The papal condemnation (Quod Aliquantum, 10 Mar 1791): Vatican Archives. The connection to the Vendée: explicitly documented — refractory priests' influence on the peasantry.

nodes.label: Law of 22 Prairial (10 Jun 1794) — the legal engine of the Great Terror
nodes.full: The Law of 22 Prairial strips accused counter-revolutionaries of the right to legal counsel or defence witnesses — the Revolutionary Tribunal has only two options: acquittal or death; executions surge from c.5 per day to c.29 per day; the Great Terror (June–July 1794) follows; Robespierre falls on 9 Thermidor partly because the law terrifies the Convention itself.
nodes.src: Law of 22 Prairial: Archives parlementaires, Vol.XCI; Moniteur Universel (BnF). Linton (2013), Choosing Terror, ch.10: the standard modern study. The execution statistics (before and after 22 Prairial): Greer (1935), The Incidence of the Terror: the quantitative study. The connection to Thermidor: the Convention members' fear that they were next — documented in multiple memoirs. The Tribunal records showing the acceleration: Archives nationales, série W.

nodes.label: Concordat of 1801 — Napoleon re-establishes the Church
nodes.full: Napoleon signs a Concordat with Pope Pius VII re-establishing the Catholic Church in France — it heals the Revolutionary schism, the Church accepts the loss of its confiscated property; still in force in Alsace-Moselle today.
nodes.src: Concordat text 15 Jul 1801: Archives nationales (AF IV 1851). The negotiation: Consalvi's memoirs (Vatican Archives). Still in force in Alsace-Lorraine (returned from Germany after 1918): documented in French law. Ellis (2000), Napoleon: the standard English biography, ch.6 on the Concordat's strategic purpose.

nodes.label: Code Napoléon — the Civil Code of 1804
nodes.full: The Code Civil (Code Napoléon) is promulgated on 21 March 1804 — 2,281 articles codifying civil law, property rights, contracts and family law; it remains the basis of French law and has been adopted or influenced law codes in 70+ countries.
nodes.src: Code Civil des Français: Bulletin des Lois, No.3909, 21 Mar 1804. Napoleon's personal role in the drafting sessions: documented in the Conseil d'État procès-verbaux (Archives nationales). Halpérin (1992), L'Impossible Code Civil: the standard study of its drafting. Current use in 70+ countries: documented by the Conseil constitutionnel's comparative law studies.

nodes.label: Dechristianisation — Reason replaces God
nodes.full: The Terror's dechristianisation campaign converts churches to Temples of Reason, abolishes Sunday, renames months, and executes priests — Notre-Dame de Paris becomes a Temple of Reason on 10 November 1793; Robespierre then institutes the Cult of the Supreme Being.
nodes.src: The ceremony at Notre-Dame 10 Nov 1793 (20 Brumaire Year II): Moniteur Universel 12 Nov 1793 (BnF). The dechristianisation decrees: Archives parlementaires. The Revolutionary calendar (introduced 22 Sep 1792): Bulletin des Lois. Vovelle (1988), The Revolution Against the Church: the standard study. The Cult of the Supreme Being festival 8 Jun 1794: Moniteur Universel.

nodes.label: Jacques-Louis David — painter of the Revolution and Empire
nodes.full: David paints The Death of Marat (1793) — the Revolution's most powerful image; becomes Napoleon's official painter (The Coronation of Napoleon, 1807); his career from the Ancien Régime through Revolution to Empire is the most complete artistic document of the entire period.
nodes.src: Death of Marat (1793): Musées Royaux des Beaux-Arts, Brussels. The Coronation of Napoleon (1807): Louvre (INV 1270). David's revolutionary activities: Archives nationales, série F17. His official commission records: Archives nationales, série O2 (Maison de l'Empéreur). Johnson (1993), Jacques-Louis David: Art in Metamorphosis: the standard study.

nodes.label: La Marseillaise (1792) — the auditory revolution
nodes.full: Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle composes the Chant de Guerre pour l'Armée du Rhin on the night of 25–26 April 1792 in Strasbourg — it reaches Paris via the Marseille volunteers (hence the name); adopted as the national anthem in 1795; it is the auditory rallying cry of the revolutionary armies and the defining musical primary source of the period.
nodes.src: Rouget de Lisle's autograph manuscript of the Marseillaise: BnF (Ms.fr.11748). Composed night of 25–26 April 1792: documented in his own account. Adopted as national anthem 14 July 1795: Moniteur Universel. Tiersot (1915), Histoire de la Marseillaise: the standard musical study. The Marseille volunteers' role: documented in the military correspondence (Archives de la Guerre). The anthem's suspension under Napoleon and restoration: documented in official decrees.

nodes.label: Beethoven's Eroica — Napoleon as muse and disappointment
nodes.full: Beethoven composes his Third Symphony dedicated to Napoleon — then, on hearing Napoleon had declared himself Emperor, tears off the dedication page and re-titles it simply 'Heroic Symphony'; the torn page survives, documenting the Enlightenment's disillusionment with Napoleon.
nodes.src: The torn dedication page (autograph score): Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, Vienna — the most famous crossed-out dedication in music history. Beethoven's letter about Napoleon to his pupil Ries: documented in Schindler (1840), Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven. First performance (private) 9 Jun 1804, Vienna: documented. Cooper (2000), Beethoven: the standard biography.

nodes.label: Arc de Triomphe and the Napoleonic building programme
nodes.full: Napoleon orders the Arc de Triomphe on 2 December 1806 (first anniversary of Austerlitz) — 50 metres high, the largest triumphal arch in the world; completed under Louis-Philippe; it lists 660 generals' names and 128 battles; the building programme transforms Paris.
nodes.src: Commission decree 2 Dec 1806: Archives nationales AF IV. Architect Chalgrin's plans: Archives nationales, Cartes et Plans. The arch's completion 1836: documented in construction records. The list of battles and generals: extant on the arch. Tulard (1985), Paris sous Louis XIV: contextualises the Napoleonic building programme.

nodes.label: What Is the Third Estate? — Sieyès launches the Revolution
nodes.full: Abbé Sieyès's pamphlet Qu'est-ce que le tiers état? (January 1789) asks and answers its own question: 'Everything. What has it been until now in the political order? Nothing. What does it want? To become something' — the founding manifesto of the Revolution.
nodes.src: Qu'est-ce que le tiers état?: published January 1789, Paris; BnF. 30,000 copies sold within weeks: documented in publisher's records. Sieyès's papers: Archives nationales, 284AP. Forsyth (1987), Reason and Revolution: The Political Thought of the Abbé Sieyès: the standard study.

nodes.label: Robespierre — 'On the Principles of Political Morality' (Feb 1794)
nodes.full: Robespierre's speech of 5 February 1794 formulates the intellectual justification of the Terror: 'virtue without terror is powerless; terror without virtue is blind'; it argues that democracy and moral virtue require terror against its enemies as their necessary instrument; the foundational text in the history of revolutionary totalitarianism.
nodes.src: Archives parlementaires (5 Feb 1794): the verbatim record — Vol.LXXXIV. Moniteur Universel 7 Feb 1794 (BnF): published text. Linton (2013), Choosing Terror: Virtue, Friendship and Authenticity in the French Revolution: the standard modern study. The speech's relationship to the Law of 22 Prairial (4 months later): documented — the same logic. Hannah Arendt, On Revolution (1963): the canonical analysis of this text in the tradition of totalitarian thought.

nodes.label: The Bulletins de la Grande Armée — Napoleon's self-narration
nodes.full: Napoleon writes or dictates 29 Bulletins de la Grande Armée — official campaign reports, published in the Moniteur, combining genuine military information with propaganda; the 29th Bulletin (1812) contains the famous line about the Russian campaign: 'The Emperor's health has never been better'.
nodes.src: Bulletins: Archives nationales AF IV; published in Moniteur Universel. The 29th Bulletin (3 Dec 1812): Moniteur 17 Dec 1812 (BnF) — 'La santé de Sa Majesté n'a jamais été meilleure.' As primary sources: the Bulletins' reliability must be assessed against other records (they systematically undercount French losses). Bret (2004), Napoleon's Bulletins: the primary analytical study.

nodes.label: The assignats — revolutionary paper money and hyperinflation
nodes.full: The National Assembly issues assignats (paper currency backed by confiscated Church property) — by 1796 they have lost 97% of their face value through overprinting; the hyperinflation is the most dramatic monetary collapse in pre-modern European history.
nodes.src: Assignat issue decrees: Archives parlementaires. Seymour Harris (1930), The Assignats: the standard economic study, with tables documenting the devaluation. The surviving assignat collection: BnF (Cabinet des médailles). The total face value issued: documented in Treasury records (Archives nationales, série Q). The connection between assignat collapse and the end of the Terror: argued by Schama (1989).

nodes.label: Maximum General (29 Sep 1793) — price controls backed by the guillotine
nodes.full: The Maximum General fixes the maximum price of grain, flour and basic necessities — backed by the penalty of death for hoarding; it pits urban consumers (sans-culottes) against rural producers; it temporarily controls inflation but creates massive black markets and shortages; abolished in December 1794 after Thermidor.
nodes.src: Law of 29 Sep 1793 (Maximum général): Archives parlementaires; Moniteur Universel 30 Sep 1793 (BnF). Aftalion (1987), The French Revolution: An Economic Interpretation: the standard economic study. Harris (1930), 'Assignats and Prices in France, 1789–1796', American Economic Review: quantifies the inflation context. The sans-culotte vs peasant conflict over the Maximum: documented in the sectional assembly records (Archives nationales, série AA). The abolition of the Maximum (24 Dec 1794): Moniteur Universel.

nodes.label: Continental System — economic war against Britain
nodes.full: Napoleon's Berlin Decree (21 November 1806) closes all French-controlled ports to British goods — an attempted total economic blockade; it damages British trade but destroys French commerce too; Portugal's refusal to join triggers the Peninsular War; Russia's breach helps cause the 1812 invasion.
nodes.src: Berlin Decree 21 Nov 1806: Archives nationales AF IV; Moniteur Universel 22 Nov 1806 (BnF). The system's economic effects: Crouzet (1964), Wars, Blockade and Economic Change in Europe 1792–1815, JEH 24: the standard economic analysis. Portugal's refusal: AGS Estado (the connection to the Peninsular War folio). The Russian breach 1810: documented in diplomatic archives.

nodes.label: The Revolution exports itself — European resonance
nodes.full: The French Revolution immediately resonates across Europe — Paine writes Rights of Man (1791), Wollstonecraft writes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), Kościuszko leads a Polish uprising (1794) citing the Declaration; the revolutionary ideas travel through pamphlets, newspapers and refugees.
nodes.src: Thomas Paine, Rights of Man (1791–1792): British Library. Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792): BL. Kościuszko's proclamation (24 Mar 1794): citing the French Declaration — Polish State Archives. The network of Jacobin clubs outside France: documented in Archives nationales, série F7. Kates (1998), The French Revolution: Recent Debates and New Controversies.

nodes.label: The Metric System (1795–1799) — global standardisation from the Revolution
nodes.full: The National Assembly commissions scientists Delambre and Méchain to measure the meridian arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona to define the metre — adopted legally on 7 April 1795; the platinum metre bar deposited in 1799; the most lasting global exchange of the Revolution; the metric system eventually becomes the universal scientific and commercial language.
nodes.src: Adoption decree 7 Apr 1795: Archives parlementaires; Moniteur Universel. The platinum metre bar (1799): Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, Sèvres (extant). Delambre (1806–1810), Base du Système Métrique Décimal (3 vols): the expedition's own account — the primary scientific documentation. Alder (2002), The Measure of All Things: the standard modern account. The international adoption: by 1900, 35 countries use the metric system — documented.

nodes.label: Napoleon's looting of European art — the Louvre as world museum
nodes.full: Napoleon's armies systematically remove art from conquered territories — 506 works from Italy (1796–1797), Egyptian antiquities, hundreds of paintings from Spain; the Louvre becomes the world's first universal museum; most works are returned after Waterloo but many remain.
nodes.src: The Italian armistice terms (1796) demanding art works: Archives des Affaires Étrangères. The inventory of works seized: Archives des musées nationaux (Louvre). The 1815 return negotiations: Archives des Affaires Étrangères. McClellan (1994), Inventing the Louvre: the standard study of the museum's Revolutionary origins. The works not returned: documented in Louvre inventories.

nodes.label: Napoleon reshapes the map of Europe
nodes.full: At its peak in 1810–1811, Napoleon's empire directly controls 70 million people across Europe — Holy Roman Empire dissolved (1806), Confederation of the Rhine, Kingdom of Westphalia; the map of Europe is redrawn more dramatically than at any point since the Roman Empire.
nodes.src: The dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire 6 Aug 1806: the Emperor's renunciation document — Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, Vienna. The map of Napoleonic Europe: documented in the treaties series (Archives des Affaires Étrangères). Broers (2002), Europe Under Napoleon: the standard study of the empire's administration.

nodes.label: Louisiana Purchase (1803) — Napoleon ends French North America
nodes.full: After the failure of the Saint-Domingue expedition, Napoleon recognises France cannot defend Louisiana against Britain — he sells the entire territory to the United States for 60 million francs on 30 April 1803; this doubles the size of the US, ends French imperial ambitions in North America, and funds Napoleon's European wars.
nodes.src: Louisiana Purchase treaty 30 Apr 1803: US National Archives (Washington); French ratification in Archives des Affaires Étrangères. The connection to Saint-Domingue: documented — Napoleon's letter to Talleyrand (January 1803) acknowledges the connection. DeConde (1976), This Affair of Louisiana: the standard study. The price: 60 million francs (15 million dollars at the time) — documented. The US Senate ratification (24 Oct 1803): documented. The territory's size: 2.1 million km² — doubles the US.

nodes.label: Olympe de Gouges — Declaration of the Rights of Woman
nodes.full: Olympe de Gouges publishes the Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne in September 1791 — mirroring the 1789 Declaration article by article to argue women have the same rights as men; she is guillotined in November 1793; her text is the founding document of modern feminism.
nodes.src: Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne (Sep 1791): BnF. Her trial records: Archives nationales, Tribunal Révolutionnaire série W. Executed 3 Nov 1793: Moniteur Universel 4 Nov 1793 (BnF). Blanc (2003), Olympe de Gouges: the standard biography. The Declaration's text: explicitly parallels the 1789 Declaration — 'Article I: Woman is born free and lives equal to man in her rights.'

nodes.label: Penal Code 1791 — homosexuality decriminalised in France
nodes.full: The Revolutionary Penal Code of 1791 removes sodomy from the list of crimes — France becomes the first major European country to decriminalise same-sex acts; the Penal Code of 1810 (the Code pénal — distinct from the Napoleonic Code / Civil Code of 1804) maintains this decriminalisation; the CATEGORICAL SHIFT is the logical extension of 'crimes without victims' Enlightenment philosophy.
nodes.src: Penal Code 1791: Archives parlementaires, Vol.XXVI. The Napoleonic Penal Code 1810: Bulletin des Lois — maintains the 1791 decriminalisation. Crompton (1985), Byron and Greek Love, ch.1: analyses the 1791 decriminalisation. Sibalis (1996), 'The Regulation of Male Homosexuality in Revolutionary and Napoleonic France' in Merrick & Ragan (eds.): the primary scholarly study. France maintained decriminalisation throughout the 19th–20th century until today.

nodes.label: Sans-culottes — the lived politics of the street
nodes.full: The sans-culottes (literally 'without breeches' — wearing working-class trousers instead of aristocratic knee-breeches) are the radical working-class militants who drive the Revolution's radicalisation through sectional assembly politics, bread riots and armed insurrections; their daily struggle with soaring bread prices, their distinct egalitarian dress and their September 1792 prison massacres are the lived politics of the street.
nodes.src: Sectional assembly records: Archives nationales, série AA — the primary source for sans-culotte political activity. Soboul (1958), Les Sans-Culottes Parisiens en l'An II: the standard study, using the sectional archives. The September Massacres 1792: documented in the Tribunal criminel records. Bread price data: documented in Labrousse (1933), Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France. The sans-culotte dress code: documented in municipal decrees and police reports.

nodes.label: Levée en masse (23 Aug 1793) — the first modern national draft
nodes.full: The Levée en masse places the entire French population at the service of the war effort — all unmarried men 18–25 are conscripted; married men forge weapons; women sew tents; children make bandages; old men preach republican virtue in public squares; the first modern total-mobilisation draft transforms the social fabric and generates massive domestic resistance.
nodes.src: Decree of the Levée en masse 23 Aug 1793: Archives parlementaires; Moniteur Universel 24 Aug 1793 (BnF). Forrest (1989), Conscripts and Deserters: the standard study of the draft's social impact. The desertion and evasion rates: documented in Archives de la Guerre A1 — approximately 20–30% of conscripts evaded. The resistance in the Vendée and elsewhere: documented connection. The decree's text: one of the most famous documents in French military history — reprinted in every standard source.
